content: A plantar wart is a type of wart caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV). It is a small lesion that develops on the sole of the foot, deriving its name from the Latin term planta pedis, meaning the sole of the foot. These warts often resemble a cauliflower in appearance. They may contain small black dots, which are actually abnormal capillaries that can bleed when the surface of the wart is shaved. While plantar warts are specifically associated with HPV infections on the sole of the foot, the virus can infect other areas of the body, such as the palm of the hand, where the warts may appear similar to plantar warts. Due to the pressure exerted on the sole of the foot, a layer of hard skin often forms over the wart. Plantar warts can be painful, but this is not always the case. They are commonly spread in communal areas such as showers, swimming pools, or through shared footwear. HPV types 1, 2, 4, and 63 are classified as clinical types, meaning they cause visible symptoms. The virus infects the skin through direct contact, typically entering through small cuts or abrasions in the outermost layer of the skin, known as the stratum corneum. After infection, warts may not become visible for several weeks or even months. On the sole of the foot, the pressure can push the wart inward, leading to the formation of a hard skin layer over it. Warts can spread through autoinoculation, infecting nearby skin or surfaces that come into contact with the infected area. They may also cluster together to form mosaic warts. Plantar warts are benign epithelial tumors caused by HPV types 1, 2, 4, or 63. Warts can spread from one part of the body to another and, less commonly, from one person to another. Infection typically occurs on moist surfaces such as communal showers, swimming pools, or inside shoes. The virus is highly contagious and can survive for months without a host. It is estimated that 7-10% of the U.S. population is infected with HPV, with a higher prevalence (29%) among individuals who have never worn shoes. Common warts generally do not cause discomfort unless they are located in areas subject to repeated friction or pressure. Plantar warts, however, can become extremely painful, especially if present in large numbers, which may interfere with walking or running. Some warts resolve spontaneously without treatment, but this process can take years. Even after disappearing, warts often recur. A typical wart appears as a raised, round, or oval growth on the skin with a rough surface. Compared to the surrounding normal skin, warts may appear lighter, darker, or even black in rare cases. Most adults are familiar with the appearance of common warts and can recognize them easily. However, unusual warts, such as those with smooth surfaces or flat warts in children, may be more challenging to identify. No treatment for warts is 100% effective. The most comprehensive medical reviews indicate that no treatment method achieves more than a 73% success rate, while placebo treatments have an average success rate of 27%. Warts can spread from one part of the body to another. Unsightly or painful warts can be treated, but warts around or under the nails are particularly difficult to cure compared to those in other locations. Although immunization is available for HPV strains associated with cervical cancer and genital warts, there is currently no vaccine for plantar warts.
